questions.question: Explain the different types of indexes in MongoDB — compound, sparse, partial, and TTL — and how you use them in a Spring Boot application.
questions.title: MongoDB Indexes: Compound, Sparse, Partial, TTL
questions.direct_answer: MongoDB indexes are **B-tree structures** that let the query planner skip collection scans. **Compound indexes** cover multiple fields and follow the **ESR rule** (Equality → Sort → Range) so the leading fields are the most selective. **Sparse indexes** include only documents where the field exists — great for optional fields and for sparse-unique constraints. **Partial indexes** are stricter: a `partialFilterExpression` picks exactly which documents to index (active users only, unshipped orders). **TTL indexes** auto-delete documents after `expireAfterSeconds`, perfect for sessions and log data. In Spring Data MongoDB you declare them with `@Indexed`, `@CompoundIndex`, or programmatically via `MongoTemplate.indexOps()`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can choose the right index type for an access pattern and understand the ESR rule and trade-offs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing sparse with partial indexes, ignoring the ESR rule on compound-index field ordering, or assuming TTL deletes immediately
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the ESR rule, name the difference between sparse and partial indexes, cover multikey limits (only one array field in a compound), and reference `explain('executionStats')`

sections.title: Why Indexes Matter
sections.content:
Without indexes, MongoDB executes a **collection scan (COLLSCAN)** — reading every document — which is O(N) and unacceptable at production scale. An index is an ordered B-tree that lets the planner pick an **IXSCAN** returning matches in sorted order with only the pages that contain them.

MongoDB supports **single-field, compound, multikey, text, geospatial, hashed, sparse, partial, and TTL** indexes.
- The most common and impactful are **compound** (multi-field, ESR-rule ordering), **sparse** (only index documents that have the field), **partial** (index only documents matching a filter), and **TTL** (auto-expire documents).
- Picking the right combination for each access pattern is the most important database-tuning skill in MongoDB.

sections.title: The ESR Rule for Compound Indexes
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    query["Query plan"] --> equality["Equality fields first (selective exact match)"]
    equality --> sort["Sort fields next (index order matches sort)"]
    sort --> range["Range fields last (reduces scan width)"]
    example["Example index { status: 1, createdAt: -1, total: 1 }"] --> equality
    example --> sort
    example --> range
```

sections.title: Single and Compound Indexes (ESR Rule)
Sparse vs Partial Indexes
TTL Indexes for Auto-Expiry
Multikey, Hashed, and Declaring in Spring Data
Index Costs
sections.content:
**When more indexes help:**
- Read-heavy workloads with known access paths
- Queries with ESR-compliant predicates
- Sort and range queries that the right index can serve from memory

**When they hurt:**
- Every index slows writes — each insert/update rewrites all relevant indexes
- Over-indexing bloats working set; RAM evicts useful pages
- Unused indexes still pay the write tax — audit regularly with `$indexStats`

**Watch for:**
- Index prefix mismatch — plan shows COLLSCAN where you expected IXSCAN
- Multikey explosion — huge arrays create huge index sizes
- Sparse index doesn't help when the query lacks the field predicate
- Background vs foreground builds — use `createIndexes` commands that don't block in 4.2+

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **ESR rule**: compound-index field order is Equality → Sort → Range
- **Sparse** indexes skip documents missing the field; **partial** indexes use a filter expression
- **TTL** auto-expires documents on a single-field date index
- **Multikey** indexes arrays; only one array field per compound index
- **`explain('executionStats')`** verifies IXSCAN vs COLLSCAN and key-examination ratio
- **Every index slows writes** — audit unused with `$indexStats`
- **Spring Data** offers `@Indexed` / `@CompoundIndex`; prefer explicit migrations for production

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Explain the index model**
- B-tree structures that avoid collection scans
- Without them, every query is O(N)

**Cover the core types**
- Compound + ESR: Equality, Sort, Range order
- Sparse: skip docs missing the field (also sparse-unique trick)
- Partial: stricter filter expression — prefer this for new indexes
- TTL: auto-expire after `expireAfterSeconds`, single-field date
- Multikey: automatic on arrays, one array per compound index

**Mention the costs**
- Every index slows writes
- Unused indexes still pay the tax — audit with `$indexStats`
- Use `explain('executionStats')` to confirm IXSCAN and the key-to-doc ratio

**Wrap up with Spring Data**
- `@Indexed`, `@CompoundIndex`, or `MongoTemplate.indexOps()` programmatic
- Use migration scripts for reviewable index changes in production

questions.question: What are covered queries in MongoDB, how does the ESR rule drive compound-index design, and how do you verify with `explain()`?
questions.title: MongoDB Covered Queries and the ESR Rule
questions.direct_answer: A **covered query** is served entirely from an index — filter, sort, and projection all hit index fields, so MongoDB never fetches the document body. The `explain()` plan shows `IXSCAN` → `PROJECTION_COVERED` with **no `FETCH` stage**. Achieving it requires a **compound index that contains every field the query reads** and **excluding `_id`** from projection unless it is in the index. The **ESR rule** (Equality → Sort → Range) drives field order: put exact-match predicates first, sort fields next, then range fields. Covered queries are the fastest possible read in MongoDB — they stay in RAM, never touch the document cache, and scale linearly with index size.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the difference between index-hitting and covered queries and can design for the fastest read path
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking any IXSCAN is 'covered', or leaving `_id: 1` in projection and losing coverage
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Walk through an `explain('executionStats')` output, show ESR-compliant index design, and name the FETCH-stage absence as the signal of coverage

sections.title: Covered Query Definition
sections.content:
A **covered query** is one where the index alone answers the query — filter, sort, and returned fields all live in the same index, so MongoDB never loads the document body from disk. It is the fastest read shape in MongoDB because the working set is limited to index pages, which are much smaller and more cacheable than full documents.

Three conditions must hold:
- Every filter field is in the index
- Every projected field is in the index
- `_id` is either in the index or explicitly excluded from the projection

Covered queries matter for **hot paths**: login lookups, autocomplete, dashboard counts, and anywhere p99 latency must stay below a few milliseconds. Pair them with **ESR-ordered compound indexes** and validate with `explain('executionStats')` to ensure the plan never falls into a `FETCH` stage.

sections.title: Designing a Covered Query
Verifying with `explain('executionStats')`
Common Reasons Coverage Breaks
sections.content:
**Projection includes a non-indexed field**
- Adding `customer: 1` forces a `FETCH` — document body must be loaded

**`_id` left in projection without being in the index**
- `_id: 1` is the default; explicitly set `_id: 0` to drop it

**Filter uses a field outside the index**
- Even one extra predicate triggers a `FETCH`

**Sort direction mismatches the index**
- Index on `{ createdAt: -1 }` supports `sort({ createdAt: -1 })` and reverse scan for `sort({ createdAt: 1 })`
- Mixed direction within a compound sort needs an exact match index

**Multikey on the indexed field**
- If the index is multikey (array field), MongoDB generally cannot cover the query — it needs the document to resolve array semantics

sections.title: Covered vs Uncovered vs Collection Scan
sections.content:
| Plan stage | Docs examined | Typical latency | When |
|---|---|---|---|
| `COLLSCAN` | All documents | very high | No usable index |
| `IXSCAN` + `FETCH` | Matching docs | medium | Index filters but projection/sort needs doc |
| `IXSCAN` + `PROJECTION_COVERED` | 0 | lowest | All fields in index, _id excluded |
| `IXSCAN` + `FETCH` + `SORT` | Matching docs + sort mem | high | Sort not matching index order |

sections.title: Covering in Production
sections.content:
**When covering helps:**
- Hot-path reads under tight latency SLO
- Tiny projections (id + 2–3 fields)
- Dashboards with repetitive queries
- High-QPS autocomplete / login checks

**When it hurts:**
- Every additional indexed field slows writes
- Wide projections force wide indexes — bloat and RAM pressure
- Multikey indexes generally can't cover — arrays complicate it

**Watch for:**
- Coverage breaks silently when someone adds a field to the projection
- Schema evolution adding a field to a doc while queries still project fewer fields — still covered, still safe
- Monitor with `$indexStats` to confirm the covering index sees traffic

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Covered query = index serves filter + sort + projection**, no document fetch
- **ESR rule**: Equality → Sort → Range index field order
- **Drop `_id`** from projection unless it is in the index
- **`PROJECTION_COVERED` + absent `FETCH` stage** in `explain()` confirms coverage
- **`totalDocsExamined: 0`** is the definitive signal
- **Multikey indexes** (arrays) typically break coverage
- **Every indexed field slows writes** — cover only hot-path queries

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Define coverage**
- Covered query: index alone answers filter + sort + projection
- Fastest possible read in MongoDB

**Apply the ESR rule**
- Equality predicates first, sort fields next, range fields last
- Include projected fields so no fetch is needed
- Drop `_id` from projection unless it's in the index

**Verify with explain**
- `PROJECTION_COVERED` wraps `IXSCAN`
- No `FETCH` stage
- `totalDocsExamined: 0`

**Close with trade-offs**
- Every covering index slows writes
- Multikey generally breaks coverage
- Use `$indexStats` to confirm traffic

questions.question: MongoDB text indexes vs Atlas Search — when is the built-in text index enough and when do you upgrade?
questions.title: MongoDB Text Indexes vs Atlas Search
questions.direct_answer: **Text indexes** are MongoDB's built-in full-text feature — create an index of type `"text"` and query with `$text`/`$search`. They are simple, work on any deployment, and do stemming in a handful of languages, but they support **only one text index per collection**, no fuzzy matching, no autocomplete, and limited relevance tuning. **Atlas Search** runs Lucene inside Atlas, auto-syncs from the oplog, and gives you **BM25 scoring, fuzzy, autocomplete, custom analyzers, facets, highlighting, and vector search** via the `$search` aggregation stage. Use text indexes for basic keyword search on self-hosted MongoDB; use Atlas Search whenever you need anything beyond simple matching.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can pick between legacy text indexes and Atlas Search based on feature depth and deployment
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using text indexes for production search workloads, or assuming Atlas Search requires a separate Elasticsearch cluster
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the one-text-index-per-collection limit, BM25 vs TF-IDF scoring difference, `$search` aggregation stage, and Atlas Vector Search for embeddings

sections.title: Two Different Generations
sections.content:
MongoDB **text indexes** were the original full-text feature — a specialized index type that tokenizes string fields, applies simple stemming, and answers `$text` queries with a basic TF-IDF-like score. They run anywhere MongoDB runs and require no extra infrastructure.

**Atlas Search** is the modern replacement — Apache Lucene embedded in Atlas cluster nodes, auto-synced from the oplog, exposed through the `$search` aggregation stage. It gives you BM25 scoring, fuzzy matching, autocomplete, custom analyzers, faceting, highlighting, compound queries, and vector search — everything you would expect from Elasticsearch, without a separate cluster.

The decision is rarely close: text indexes are a low-featured fallback for self-hosted MongoDB; Atlas Search is what you use on Atlas the moment search matters.

sections.title: Text Indexes in Action
Atlas Search in Action
Text Index vs Atlas Search
sections.content:
| Feature | Text Index | Atlas Search |
|---|---|---|
| Engine | Custom | Apache Lucene |
| Scoring | TF-IDF-like | BM25 + custom functions |
| Fuzzy | No | Yes (`fuzzy.maxEdits`) |
| Autocomplete | No | Yes (edgeGram tokenizer) |
| Analyzers | Limited language list | Lucene + custom |
| Synonyms | No | Yes |
| Highlighting | No | Yes |
| Faceting | No | Yes |
| Vector search | No | Yes (knnVector + `$vectorSearch`) |
| Indexes per collection | 1 | Many |
| Deployment | Anywhere | Atlas only |
| Composes with pipeline | `$text` match only | Full `$search` stage + compound |

sections.title: Picking the Right Tool
sections.content:
**When text indexes are enough:**
- Self-hosted MongoDB where Atlas Search isn't available
- Basic keyword search on a small set of documents
- No fuzzy, no autocomplete, no relevance tuning

**When Atlas Search is the answer:**
- Autocomplete or typo-tolerance required
- Custom analyzers (stemming, normalization, synonyms)
- Faceting or highlighting for search UI
- Vector search for semantic / RAG workloads
- Multiple search shapes per collection

**Watch for:**
- Text indexes limit — one per collection
- Atlas Search dedicated search nodes recommended at > 500 QPS to isolate load
- Reindex strategy when the mapping changes
- Search-specific scaling separate from primary workload

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Text indexes** are MongoDB's built-in basic full-text; one per collection
- **Atlas Search** is Lucene in Atlas with `$search` stage and auto-sync from oplog
- **BM25**, fuzzy, autocomplete, facets, highlight, synonyms are Atlas-only
- **Atlas Vector Search** enables semantic / RAG workloads with `$vectorSearch`
- **`$search` aggregation stage** composes with the rest of the pipeline
- **Dedicated search nodes** recommended at high QPS to isolate load
- **Pick text indexes only for self-hosted basic search**; otherwise Atlas Search

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Contrast the two generations**
- Text indexes: basic, anywhere, one per collection, TF-IDF-like
- Atlas Search: Lucene in Atlas, BM25, fuzzy, autocomplete, facets, vector

**Cover the decision**
- Self-hosted + basic keyword → text index
- Anything beyond simple matching → Atlas Search
- RAG / semantic retrieval → Atlas Vector Search via `$vectorSearch`

**Show the ergonomic win**
- `$search` stage composes with the rest of the pipeline
- No separate Elasticsearch cluster to run

**Close**
- Dedicated search nodes at high QPS to isolate load
- Mapping changes require a reindex — plan blue/green
